issues.legal_issue: Considering officials’ comments on an employee’s response to a proposed punishment without separately disclosing those comments does not violate natural justice where the employee knew comments would be made, the comments introduce no new facts, and the employee had an opportunity to address the evidence.
material_facts: The employee was told that two officials would comment on his response to the proposed dismissal and that their comments would be forwarded to the deciding authority.
He did not ask for the comments to be disclosed or request an opportunity to answer them.
The comments addressed his response to the proposed punishment and did not introduce facts outside the record.
The underlying evidence had been presented in his presence, and he had an opportunity to meet it; the full record was also available to him on appeal.
issues.conclusion: The consideration of the officials’ comments did not violate the principles of natural justice.
issues.legal_principle: Natural justice did not require a further opportunity to respond in these circumstances: the employee knew comments would be made, did not request disclosure or an opportunity to answer, and the comments contained no new or undisclosed facts. The judgment relies on no earlier case for this conclusion.

rule.if: disciplinary_dismissal_review and employee_knew_comments_would_be_made and no_request_to_answer_comments and comments_added_no_new_facts and opportunity_to_meet_record_evidence

predicates.disciplinary_dismissal_review: The matter concerns review of an employee’s dismissal following a disciplinary proceeding.
predicates.employee_knew_comments_would_be_made: The employee was informed that officials would comment on the employee’s response to the proposed punishment.
predicates.no_request_to_answer_comments: The employee did not ask to see the comments or request an opportunity to answer them.
predicates.comments_added_no_new_facts: The officials’ comments addressed the employee’s response and introduced no facts beyond the existing record.
predicates.opportunity_to_meet_record_evidence: The employee had an opportunity to address the evidence in the record, and the record was available during the appeal.

issues.definition: When an employee knows comments will be made, does not seek an opportunity to answer them, and the comments add no new facts to evidence the employee could address, considering those comments does not violate natural justice.

issues.legal_issue: A disciplinary finding against an employee responsible for making land-settlement recommendations is supported by evidence and cannot be avoided on the ground that the employee performed only a ministerial forwarding function when the evidence shows improper settlements and the employee’s duties required independent field verification.
material_facts: The disciplinary charge concerned recommendations for settling lands in favour of persons who were not tenants and did not belong to the village where the lands were situated.
Reports and testimony provided evidence supporting the finding that the proposed beneficiaries were not in possession of the lands as tenants.
The employee maintained that he had acted mechanically on subordinate officers’ reports and that his function was ministerial.
The applicable service rules described Kanungos as executive revenue officers expected to spend much of their time on outdoor work in the field.
issues.conclusion: The finding on the principal charge was supported by evidence, and the employee could not disclaim responsibility as a mere forwarding agency.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 145 of the Board’s Miscellaneous Rules described Kanungos as executive revenue officers expected to undertake outdoor work in the field. In light of that duty, an officer making recommendations about rent abatement and settlement with new tenants had to inspect the locality and satisfy himself that the reports complied with the rules; his responsibility was not merely ministerial. The evidence that the beneficiaries were neither local nor tenants also defeated the claim that the finding rested on no evidence.

rule.if: disciplinary_misconduct_review and employee_made_land_settlement_recommendations and clear_evidence_of_improper_beneficiaries and role_required_field_verification and employee_claimed_only_forwarding_role

predicates.disciplinary_misconduct_review: The matter concerns review of a disciplinary finding against an employee.
predicates.employee_made_land_settlement_recommenda: The employee made recommendations concerning the settlement of land with new tenants.
predicates.clear_evidence_of_improper_beneficiaries: Evidence showed that the recommended beneficiaries were not tenants in possession and did not belong to the locality.
predicates.role_required_field_verification: The employee’s official role required executive field work and checking that settlement reports were justified.
predicates.employee_claimed_only_forwarding_role: The employee maintained that he had merely passed on subordinate officers’ reports without independent responsibility.

issues.definition: When an employee responsible for land-settlement recommendations has a field-verification duty and evidence shows the recommendations favoured persons who were not tenants, the finding is supported and the employee cannot treat the role as merely ministerial.

issues.legal_issue: Missing documents do not invalidate a disciplinary finding on a charge supported by other evidence made available to the employee where the employee had an opportunity to address that evidence and did not claim that a site visit would have made the missing documents relevant.
material_facts: Some documents were missing during the disciplinary enquiry.
The principal charge was supported by reports and testimony that were on the record and available to the employee, who had an opportunity to address them.
The employee did not claim that he had visited the land and verified that the subordinate officers’ report was correct.
The employee instead maintained that his role was merely ministerial and that the primary responsibility lay with a subordinate officer.
issues.conclusion: The missing documents did not undermine the finding on the principal charge in the circumstances of this case.
issues.legal_principle: The significance of missing documents depends on whether they could matter to the employee’s answer to the charge. Here, the principal charge rested on reports and testimony available to the employee, and the employee did not assert that he had personally inspected the site. The Court observed that such an assertion might have made the missing papers relevant, but the employee’s ministerial-role argument did not do so. The judgment relies on no earlier case for this conclusion.

rule.if: disciplinary_finding_review and some_documents_missing and principal_charge_supported_by_available_evidence and employee_had_opportunity_to_address_that_evidence and employee_did_not_claim_personal_site_verification

predicates.disciplinary_finding_review: The matter concerns review of a finding made in a disciplinary proceeding.
predicates.some_documents_missing: Some documents that might have been relevant were not available during the enquiry.
predicates.principal_charge_supported_by_available_: The principal charge was supported by reports and testimony that were on the record and available to the employee.
predicates.employee_had_opportunity_to_address_that: The employee had a full opportunity to meet the evidence supporting the principal charge.
predicates.employee_did_not_claim_personal_site_ver: The employee did not assert that he had personally visited the site and verified the subordinate officers’ report.

issues.definition: When a disciplinary charge rests on available evidence the employee could address, missing documents do not undermine the finding if the employee did not claim that personal site verification would make those documents relevant.
